study.title: Ecclesiastes 1 - The futility of life Under the sun
study.overview: The chapter opens with the voice of the Preacher, traditionally associated with Solomon, stating that everything observed in the common life is marked by transience, repetition and inability to give lasting satisfaction. First, he presents the general thesis: human work does not produce final benefit in the face of the expiry of existence. Then it uses nature as proof: generations pass, the cycles of the sun, wind and water continue without bringing fullness. Finally, the Preacher reports his own search for wisdom and knowledge; even this search, as high as possible, ends in the finding that increasing knowledge can also increase the inner weight, because human reality remains limited and frustrating.

outline.title: Registration and thesis on futility
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with the presentation of the Preagador and the central statement that everything is futile, followed by the question about the real profit of human labor. The brevity of generations shows that individual life passes without permanence proportional to the effort employed.

outline.title: The cycles of creation and the return of it
outline.explanation: The sun, the wind and the rivers illustrate a world in continuous motion, but without final advance. The observer notes tiredness, saturation of the senses, historical repetition and forgetfulness, reinforcing the idea that nothing in the earthly sphere offers lasting novelty or perennial memory.

outline.title: The Search for Wisdom and Its Pain
outline.explanation: The Preacher describes his investigation with great dedication and acknowledges that he has received this tiring occupation from God. Even after broadening his knowledge and studying wisdom, madness and foolishness, he concludes that the increase in wisdom also brings annoyance and anguish.

study.context: The notes provided indicate that the book is traditionally attributed to Solomon, son of David and King in Jerusalem, although authorship is discussed by some scholars. The text itself is presented by the voice of the Preactor, and the commentators highlight that this figure speaks from personal experience and broad reflection on the human condition. The horizon of the chapter is "under the sun" or "below the sky," an expression that delimits the analysis of observable life in this world.
study.theology: Ecclesiastes 1 teaches that creation, although ordered and continuous, was not given to be the ultimate source of meaning, satisfaction or permanence. The chapter unmasks the illusion that work, novelty, progress, historical memory or even human wisdom can solve the fundamental frustration of fallen existence. The repetition of the word translated by futility points to something like steam, blowing or water vapor: present but unstable reality and runaway. At the same time, the text does not glorify ignorance; it values the sincere pursuit of wisdom, but shows that when the creature tries to find fullness only in itself and in the world, it discovers limits, tiredness and pain. Thus, the chapter prepares the reader for a humble faith: to recognize the weakness of human life and the need to receive from God what the world cannot offer.

scholarViews.insight: The Preacher notes that the movements of nature and history have a circular rhythm of coming and going, which supports the conclusion that everything is futile or steam.
The passage over generations shows that human life is brief and passes quickly, making earthly goods unable to give lasting solidity.
The text explains that the sea does not fill itself because the water returns in cycle; the image reinforces the repetitive and incessant character of creation.

questions: What areas of your life do you treat yourself as if you can offer lasting satisfaction, though the chapter shows you are passing?
How can the repetition of natural cycles and history lead to both discouragement and humility before God?
How can the search for knowledge become a blessing, but also reveal limits and produce anguish?
study.practice: This week, note where you are looking for meaning in work, performance, consumption or recognition. Write down one or two places where you expect more than these things can give. Then take daily time for simple prayer and biblical reading, asking God to reorganize his expectations and give him wisdom with humility, instead of relying on news or achievements to have peace.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow the authorship of the book to be stated; the attribution to Solomon is traditional and likely, but remains interpretive. There is also no basis, in the notes given here, for additional historical details beyond the general framework of the text and the traditional reading of the chapter.
